name: Truganini
info: Truganini, a Nuenonne woman born around 1812 on the south-eastern coast of Tasmania, guided George Augustus Robinson's expeditions that ended in her people's exile, and was later wrongly described as the last Aboriginal Tasmanian.

facts.born: c. 1812 at Recherche Bay, southern Tasmania (then Van Diemen's Land), the youngest daughter of Manganerer, the senior man of the Nuenonne clan; her mother was likely a member of the Ninene people
facts.died: 8 May 1876 in Hobart, in the Dandridge family home, after falling into a coma on 4 May; she had contracted bronchitis the year before
facts.role: Nuenonne woman; guide to George Augustus Robinson on his expeditions of 1830 to 1836; resident of the Wybalenna Aboriginal Establishment and of Oyster Cove
facts.known: growing up on Bruny Island during British colonisation; guiding Robinson's expeditions in the Black War; exile at Wybalenna; the trial of 1841 at Melbourne; the mistaken description of her as the last Aboriginal Tasmanian; the treatment of her remains and their cremation in 1976

t: Truganini, a member of the Nuenonne people, saw her mother murdered by sailors and two of her sisters kidnapped by a sealer, and in her teens and twenties lived through the Black War between colonists and Aboriginal Tasmanians.

From 1830 she guided George Augustus Robinson on expeditions that ended in the exile of the Aboriginal people of the Tasmanian mainland, and she was herself exiled to Wybalenna on Flinders Island in 1835.

After her death the colonial government declared the island's Aboriginal population extinct, a claim scholars and the Aboriginal Tasmanian community reject, and her remains were displayed for decades against her wishes before being cremated and scattered in 1976.
dyk: Truganini twice saved Robinson's life by swimming across the Arthur River with him or towing his raft, in 1832 and 1834, yet she begged her doctor that her body not be mutilated by scientists after her death.
ev: Truganini is born at Recherche Bay, the youngest daughter of Manganerer of the Nuenonne
Robinson brings her to his mission at Missionary Bay on Bruny Island, and in October she marries Woureddy
She sets out as a guide on Robinson's "friendly mission" to the Aboriginal peoples of western and north-western Tasmania
Robinson announces that the Aboriginal population of the Tasmanian mainland has been exiled, and Truganini is taken to Wybalenna on Flinders Island
She is tried at Melbourne with four others and acquitted as an accessory; Maulboyheenner and Peevay are convicted and hanged in January 1842
The survivors at Wybalenna, Truganini among them, are moved to Oyster Cove
Truganini dies in Hobart, and the Tasmanian government declares the island's Aboriginal population extinct
Her remains, held by the Tasmanian Museum, are cremated and scattered in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel

sections.early:
Truganini was born around 1812 at Recherche Bay in southern Tasmania, then known as Van Diemen's Land. She was the youngest daughter of Manganerer, the senior man of the Nuenonne clan, whose country included Bruny Island and the coastal area of the Tasmanian mainland between Recherche Bay and Oyster Cove. Her mother, with whom Manganerer had at least three daughters, was likely a member of the Ninene people. At the beginning of the 19th century the Aboriginal population of Tasmania numbered around 3000–8000, forming nine nations divided into around 50–100 clan groups.

British colonisation had reached Nuenonne country before her birth. James Cook first landed on Bruny Island at Adventure Bay in 1777, and within a few decades former convicts were raiding Aboriginal communities to kidnap women. When French explorers and scientists visited in 1802, the Nuenonne they met were terrified of their guns. After Hobart was founded in 1804, many ships passed Nuenonne country. The seal colonies the Nuenonne relied on were soon destroyed, and many Nuenonne women were forced to trade sex for food with settlers at the whaling stations. In 1816 sailors murdered Truganini's mother, and in 1826 a sealer kidnapped two of her sisters.
sections.rise:
By the late 1820s Tasmania was in the midst of the Black War, a conflict between colonists and Aboriginal Tasmanians in which kidnapping of Aboriginal women was common and displaced Aboriginal people carried out retributive violence. In 1819 the Aboriginal and settler populations had each been around 5000, the settlers overwhelmingly male; by 1830 the settler population had grown to 23,500. According to an unverified account published shortly before Truganini's death by the surveyor James Erskine Calder, around 1828 timber cutters abducted and raped her and murdered two Nuenonne men, one of them her fiancé Paraweena.

Governor George Arthur declared martial law in the settled districts in November 1828, but not on Bruny Island, which he thought a suitable site for conciliation. He appointed George Augustus Robinson, a builder from London and a devout Christian who expressed religious and humanitarian motivations, to run a ration station there. Robinson met Truganini in April 1829 among convict woodcutters on the mainland and brought her to a mission at Missionary Bay, where he used her presence to draw her father and others. Disease soon struck the mission. Truganini left for the whaling station at Adventure Bay, but Robinson retrieved her, and after initial firm resistance she reluctantly married the Nuenonne elder Woureddy in October 1829.
sections.deeds:
In January 1830 Robinson obtained the governor's approval for a "friendly mission" to the Aboriginal peoples of western and north-western Tasmania, and Truganini went with him as a guide. The party set out from Recherche Bay on 3 February 1830. Truganini, who was suffering from advanced syphilis, collected food by diving for shellfish and gathering plants. On the way they learned of massacres in the Black War, in which about 60 settlers and 300 Aboriginal Tasmanians had been killed over the preceding two years. Tom Lawson has described the expeditions, which continued until 1834, as a "roving embassy" that eventually negotiated an end to the violent conflict.

As the governor's "Black Line" militia took the field, Robinson set out with Truganini and others to persuade groups to surrender, and they convinced some, among them the warrior Mannalargenna's group, to go to Swan Island, an exposed island with little food or clean water. Robinson later settled Aboriginal people on Gun Carriage Island and then Flinders Island, over the guides' complaints. In 1832 and 1834 Truganini saved Robinson's life at the Arthur River. In 1833 she led parties that located Ninine and Tarkiner people; many of those brought to Sarah Island died, and only a handful were alive when they were sent to Flinders Island on 20 November 1833.
sections.opponents:
Truganini and the other guides were often at odds with Robinson. They complained about being resettled on Gun Carriage Island, and Truganini refused to enter her cottage there and begged to return to the mainland. Robinson was rewarded with land grants and hundreds of pounds, while the guides received clothing and a boat that they never saw or used; Robinson rented it out and kept the proceeds in an account he controlled. At Wybalenna he changed residents' names and made them wear European clothes, renaming Truganini "Lalla Rookh". Of the 300 Aboriginal Tasmanians who had surrendered to Robinson since 1830, 112 were alive at Wybalenna in 1835, and about half of the residents died between 1835 and 1839, mostly of pneumonia.

In 1841, in the Port Phillip District, Truganini ran away from the Aboriginal encampment with Maulboyheenner, Peevay and two women. They plundered a settler's hut, and Maulboyheenner and Peevay beat and shot two whalers to death, mistaking them for members of a search party. The five were tried at Melbourne; as non-Christians they could not testify, and their counsel Redmond Barry argued that it was unfair to try an "alien people" in an unfamiliar courtroom. Truganini and the other women were acquitted; the two men were hanged on 20 January 1842 before a crowd of 4000–5000. In 1976 Vivienne Rae-Ellis published a biography presenting Truganini as a traitor who collaborated with settlers, a view other writers have contested.
sections.last:
Truganini was returned to Wybalenna in July 1842; Woureddy died on the journey, likely of syphilis. The superintendent forced her into a marriage with Mannapackername, and both rebelled. After the residents petitioned Queen Victoria and the governor, the settlement was closed in May 1847, and the 47 survivors were moved to Oyster Cove on 18 October 1847. There Truganini hunted marsupials, dived for shellfish and often returned to Bruny Island. Mortality was high, in part because of alcohol, and the residents were given mercury chloride, which likely contributed to mental illness. By 1859 only 14 Aboriginal Tasmanians were left, and in 1861 her clanswoman Dray died.

Museums and collectors began gathering remains from the settlement, and the survivors were frequently photographed. William Lanne, her partner, who was understood to be the last surviving Aboriginal Tasmanian man, died on 3 March 1869, and members of the Royal Society mutilated his body to secure his skeleton. Truganini begged a minister to see that she was buried at sea. Moved to Hobart in 1872 and cared for by the Dandridge family, she asked her doctor to have her buried "behind the mountains". She fell into a coma on 4 May 1876 and died on 8 May. Her body was buried at the Female Factory to protect it from body snatchers.
sections.legacy:
After her death the Royal Society's Secretary asked for her remains, and the government permitted only a cast of her face. In 1878, after a campaign by the society, her body was disinterred for use only in science, and about a decade later her skull was shown at the Melbourne Centennial Exhibition. In 1904 an articulated skeleton was made for display at the Tasmanian Museum. It was withdrawn from view in 1947 after campaigning, legislation in 1975 gave the government ownership, and her remains were cremated and scattered in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel in 1976. Skin and hair were returned in 2002 and 2005.

Truganini was widely, though incorrectly, described as the last surviving Aboriginal Tasmanian. Scholars and the present Aboriginal Tasmanian community reject that claim: a community descended from Aboriginal women and sealers continued on Cape Barren Island and elsewhere in the Furneaux Group, and Lyndall Ryan's 1981 book was among the first to challenge the extinction myth. Tom Lawson argues that the narrative served to reinforce British power. Clive Turnbull in 1948 portrayed her as resisting the extermination of her people; Rebe Taylor wrote that she became a symbol of white Australian guilt. Some Aboriginal people reclaim her as an anti-colonial figure. In 2009 Aboriginal Tasmanians stopped the sale at Sotheby's of copies of Benjamin Law's busts of her and Woureddy.

summary: Truganini (c. 1812–1876), a Nuenonne woman from Bruny Island, guided George Augustus Robinson's expeditions in the Black War and was exiled with her people. She was wrongly called the last Aboriginal Tasmanian, a claim scholars and the Aboriginal Tasmanian community reject.
references: Murray Johnson, Van Diemen's Land: An Aboriginal History (University of New South Wales Press, 2015)
Tom Lawson, The Last Man: A British Genocide in Tasmania (I.B. Tauris, 2014)
Cassandra Pybus, Truganini: Journey Through the Apocalypse (Allen & Unwin, 2020)
Lyndall Ryan, Tasmanian Aborigines: A History Since 1803 (Allen & Unwin, 2012)
notes: Dates: the article gives 'c. 1812' for birth and 8 May 1876 for death; circa set for the birth only.
Calder's account of the 1828 abduction and the murder of Paraweena is described by the article as unverified, and is given so.

Sarah Island: the article says the Tarkiner adults all died after being brought there, and that only a handful of Ninine and Tarkiner captives were alive when sent to Flinders Island on 20 November (the year is not stated in that sentence; it follows the 1833 expedition, so 1833 is used in 'deeds').
The Arthur River rescues: the first is placed in September 1832 and the second in 1834; stated in the dyk as 1832 and 1834.
Syphilis: the article says she was suffering an advanced case during the 1830 expedition; kept as given.

The 'opponents' section also gathers the conflicts between the guides and Robinson, since the article names no single group of opponents; the Rae-Ellis view is attributed to her and described only as contested by 'other writers', as the article treats it as controversial and revisionist.
Burial: the article says she was buried at the Female Factory to protect her from body snatchers; the 1878 disinterment is by the Royal Society's campaign.
The article has Truganini seeing the 'Black Line' only through Robinson's agreement; the 2200 militiamen figure and costs were left out.
The sentence 'Lanne, her partner' rests on the article's 'entered a relationship with a younger Aboriginal man named William Lanne'.

Left out: the rest of the Wybalenna/Oyster Cove petition details, the 1868 presentation to the Duke of Edinburgh, the cultural depictions section (paintings, songs, The Conciliation), and the 1997 returns of artefacts.
